Package com.im.njams.sdk.communication

Class AbstractSender

  • java.lang.Object
    • com.im.njams.sdk.communication.AbstractSender
  • Direct Known Subclasses:
    AbstractJmsSender, HttpSender, KafkaSender
    public abstract class AbstractSender
extends Object
    Superclass for all Senders. Extend this class to create a nJAMS sender implementation that can send project- and log-messages to the nJAMS server. When writing your own Sender, extend this class and override methods when needed. All Senders are automatically pooled by the SDK; you must not implement your own connection pooling!

    Do not implement retrying or discard-policy handling. Implement connect(), close() and the typed send methods as single honest attempts that throw on failure, and route each unit you actually put on the wire through sendWithRetry(SendAttempt) — it owns the bounded retrying, the discard policy and when a failure is escalated, consistently for every transport.

    The SDK also drives the connection lifecycle: do not implement reconnect logic — it runs exactly one reconnect per sender group. If your transport detects a broken connection asynchronously, report it with notifyConnectionFailure(Exception).

    Senders are internal SDK infrastructure, not part of the user-facing API — client applications must not use this class or obtain a sender instance directly.

    Names need not be unique: when several senders report the same name, the SDK tries them in the order their META-INF/services entries are listed and uses the first one that initializes successfully. An implementation that is not applicable in the current environment declines by throwing TransportNotApplicableException from init(ClientSettings), leaving the next one to be tried.

    Version:
    4.0.6
    Author:
    hsiegeln

      • send

        public void send​(com.faizsiegeln.njams.messageformat.v4.common.CommonMessage msg,
                 String clientSessionId)
        Dispatches the given message to the matching typed send method. One honest attempt: any failure propagates to the caller, which decides from this sender's own classification whether to retire it or merely drop the message.

        The connection is guaranteed to be established — SenderPool.acquire() only hands out connected senders — so this method does not check the connection status, retry, or apply the discard policy. Those are the pool's responsibility.

        Parameters:
        msg - the message to send
        clientSessionId - the session ID of the Njams instance that sends the message

      • sendWithRetry

        protected final void sendWithRetry​(SendAttempt attempt)
                            throws Exception
        Sends one already-built message unit, applying this SDK's retry and discard-policy handling.

        Call this once per unit a transport actually puts on the wire — per chunk when a message is split, so a failure resumes at the chunk that failed instead of re-sending the ones that already arrived. The attempt must be a single honest send that throws on failure; everything else is handled here.

        A failure this method cannot resolve locally is rethrown unchanged, so the SDK can classify the very same throwable this method classified. Congestion is the one failure retried indefinitely, on this same connection, and only while the configured policy still wants the message sent — it never reaches the caller in that case, because retiring and reconnecting a connection that is merely busy would be pure overhead. Waiting out congestion stops early if this sender's pool replaces it in the meantime: the message then belongs on the group's current connection, not on this one.

        Parameters:
        attempt - one honest send attempt.
        Throws:
        Exception - the failure that could not be resolved locally, unchanged.
        Since:
        6.1.0

      • logError

        protected void logError​(AbstractSender.SendFailureOutcome outcome,
                        Throwable failure)
        Reports a send failure and what was decided about it, so a transport can log it with the detail only it has — a status code, a destination, a broker limit. Called for every failure the SDK acts on, including the ones it retries, so an implementation must keep a repeated failure quiet (debug/trace) and reserve warn/error for an outcome that actually loses or escalates a message.

        The default logs at debug without any transport detail. Overriding is optional.

        Parameters:
        outcome - what the SDK decided about this failure.
        failure - the failure itself; may be null.
        Since:
        6.1.0

      • notifyConnectionFailure

        protected final void notifyConnectionFailure​(Exception cause)
        Reports a connection failure that was detected outside a send call, so the owning SenderPool can retire this sender and run a single reconnect for its group.

        Implement this call only if your transport can detect a broken connection asynchronously — for example from a listener callback on a transport-internal thread, with no send in progress. A failure that surfaces from a send must simply be thrown: the SDK reports it for you.

        Parameters:
        cause - the failure that was detected; may be null.

      • isCongestion

        protected abstract boolean isCongestion​(Throwable failure)
        Classifies a failure reported for this sender. Return true only for a failure that is mere congestion — short-lived and self-healing, likely to succeed again shortly without any manual intervention, such as a transport-level back-pressure signal from an otherwise healthy connection.

        A connection that is technically established but not usable for its purpose — a rejected destination, a security failure, a malformed request — is not congestion and must not return true here, even though the transport is nominally "connected".

        Part of the sender SPI: every implementation must decide this for itself, there is no inherited default. A transport that cannot positively identify congestion must simply return false — the safe choice, since it keeps the pre-classification behaviour of assuming a real connection problem.

        This method must never throw. It has to reach a decision: when it cannot — including when inspecting the failure itself goes wrong — the answer is false, the safe fallback. Callers rely on getting an answer, and the same failure is classified more than once while a send is being decided, so an implementation must also be a pure function of its argument: same throwable in, same answer out.

        Classify by inspecting the whole cause chain, not just the throwable itself: a transport's own send may wrap the failure before the SDK gets to classify it.

        Consumed to decide whether a registered SenderRecoveryListener is notified when the group recovers, by sendWithRetry(SendAttempt) to decide whether a failed send keeps applying back pressure instead of being escalated, and by the SDK to decide whether a failure it could not send retires the connection or only drops the message. It does not influence the group's own failed/reconnecting state.

        Parameters:
        failure - the failure that was reported; may be null.
        Returns:
        true only if this transport can positively identify the failure as short-lived congestion; false — the safe default — for anything it cannot positively identify as such.
        Since:
        6.1.0

      • isMessageRejected

        protected abstract boolean isMessageRejected​(Throwable failure)
        Classifies a failure reported for this sender. Return true only if retrying the exact message that failed could never succeed, regardless of the connection's state — for example, a payload the target permanently refuses to accept. A transport that identifies this discards just that one message and leaves the connection untouched, bypassing the configured NjamsSettings.PROPERTY_DISCARD_POLICY entirely: retrying forever cannot help, so discarding is preferable even under a policy that would otherwise never discard.

        Part of the sender SPI: every implementation must decide this for itself, there is no inherited default. A transport that cannot positively identify a permanent rejection must simply return false — the safe choice, since retrying might still help.

        This method must never throw. It has to reach a decision: when it cannot — including when inspecting the failure itself goes wrong — the answer is false, the safe fallback. Callers rely on getting an answer, and the same failure is classified more than once while a send is being decided, so an implementation must also be a pure function of its argument: same throwable in, same answer out.

        Classify by inspecting the whole cause chain, not just the throwable itself: a transport's own send may wrap the failure before the SDK gets to classify it.

        Parameters:
        failure - the failure that was reported; may be null.
        Returns:
        true only if this transport can positively identify the message itself as permanently unsendable; false — the safe default — for anything it cannot positively identify as such.
        Since:
        6.1.0
